units.title: Basics 1
units.description: Your very first German words and sentences. Learn people, food, drinks, and how to say what you are and what you eat or drink.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to German! 🎉

**Nouns & Gender:** Every German noun has a gender: **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine), or **das** (neuter). You must learn the article with the word — it's part of the word!

**The verb *sein* (to be):**
- ich bin — I am
- du bist — you are
- er/sie ist — he/she is

Example: *Ich bin ein Mann.* (I am a man.)

**Verbs *essen* (to eat) and *trinken* (to drink):**
- ich esse / trinke
- du isst / trinkst
- er/sie isst / trinkt

Example: *Ich esse Brot.* (I eat bread.)

**Word order:** German usually puts the verb in the **second position**. Time words like *Ich* come first, then the verb, then the rest.

**Tip:** Always capitalize nouns in German!

units.title: Greetings
units.description: Learn essential German greetings and polite expressions for everyday conversations.
units.guidebook:
## Greetings & Politeness 👋

German greetings change with the time of day:
- **Guten Morgen** (good morning) — until about noon
- **Guten Tag** (good day) — the safe all-day default
- **Guten Abend** (good evening) — from about 18:00
- **Gute Nacht** (good night) — only when parting or going to bed

**Hallo** is casual and works any time with friends. **Tschüss** is an informal goodbye; **Auf Wiedersehen** is more formal. To say "see you soon," use **Bis bald**.

When meeting someone, Germans often ask **Wie geht es Ihnen?** (formal) or **Wie geht's?** (casual). A typical reply is **Mir geht es gut, danke** ("I'm doing well, thanks").

**Bitte** means both "please" and "you're welcome" — context tells you which. **Danke** means "thanks," and **Vielen Dank** means "thank you very much." **Entschuldigung** ("excuse me") is used to get attention or apologize for small things; **Es tut mir leid** is a stronger apology.

Politeness goes a long way in German — use **Sie** (formal you) with strangers and **du** with friends and children.

units.title: Food
units.description: Learn essential German words for food and drink, and how to say what you want, eat, and drink.
units.guidebook:
## Talking About Food in German 🍽️

In this unit, you'll learn the most common food and drink words. German nouns have **genders** (der, die, das), and you must learn the article with each noun:

- **der** = masculine (e.g., *der Käse* – the cheese)
- **die** = feminine (e.g., *die Milch* – the milk)
- **das** = neuter (e.g., *das Ei* – the egg)

### Verbs for eating and drinking
- **essen** (to eat): *Ich esse Brot.* – I eat bread.
- **trinken** (to drink): *Ich trinke Kaffee.* – I drink coffee.
- **möchten** (to want): *Ich möchte Wasser.* – I would like water.

### Word order
German usually places the verb in the **second position** of a sentence. With *möchten*, the other verb goes to the end: *Ich möchte **essen**.*

### Plurals
Some plurals are irregular: *das Ei → die Eier* (eggs). Don't worry — you'll learn them with practice!

exercises.translation: I would like to drink coffee.

exercises.answer: He drinks a glass of water.

units.title: Animals
units.description: Learn the names of common animals in German and how to describe them simply.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to **Animals**! 🐾

In German, every noun has a **gender** (der/die/das), which affects the article you use. Most animals follow these patterns:
- **der** for male animals (e.g., *der Hund*)
- **die** for female animals (e.g., *die Katze*)
- **das** for baby/young animals (e.g., *das Kalb*)

To say **"the dog is big"**, use: *Der Hund ist groß.* Notice the verb **ist** (is) comes second. To make a sentence negative, add **nicht** (not) before the adjective: *Der Hund ist nicht klein.*

To describe an animal, pair a noun with an adjective like **groß** (big), **klein** (small), **schnell** (fast), or **süß** (cute). Always capitalize nouns in German! 🐴

units.title: Travel
units.description: Learn essential German vocabulary and phrases for getting around cities, taking trains, staying in hotels, and visiting museums.
units.guidebook:
## Getting Around in German 🇩🇪

**Asking where things are** is one of the most useful travel skills. Use:
- *Wo ist...?* — Where is...?
- *Wo ist der Bahnhof?* — Where is the train station?

**Getting directions** often starts with *Wie komme ich zu...?** (How do I get to...?). You can also use the imperative: *Gehen Sie geradeaus* (Go straight ahead) or *Biegen Sie links ab* (Turn left).

**At the hotel**, you'll need *Ich möchte ein Zimmer reservieren* (I would like to reserve a room). German nouns always carry a gender — *der Bahnhof* (masculine), *die Stadt* (feminine), *das Museum* (neuter) — so memorize articles with nouns!

**Compound nouns** are everywhere in German: *Flughafen* (airport) = *Flug* + *Hafen*. Recognizing parts helps you guess meanings.

**Politeness matters:** use *bitte* (please) and *danke* (thanks) often. *Entschuldigung* politely gets attention or means "excuse me."

Gute Reise! 🚆

units.title: Family
units.description: Learn how to talk about your family members, relatives, and loved ones in German.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Family

To talk about your family in German, you will use possessive words like **mein** (my) and **dein** (your). Notice how their endings change based on grammatical gender:

- **Masculine & Neuter:** *mein Vater* (my father), *mein Kind* (my child)
- **Feminine & Plural:** *meine Mutter* (my mother), *meine Eltern* (my parents)

### Informal Grandparents
While *Großmutter* and *Großvater* are standard, Germans almost always refer to their grandparents affectionately as **die Oma** (grandma) and **der Opa** (grandpa).

### Using "Haben"
When saying you have a family member, masculine words change in the accusative case: *Ich habe **einen** Bruder*, but *Ich habe **eine** Schwester*.

exercises.translation: My grandfather is reading a book.

units.title: Shopping
units.description: Learn how to navigate stores, ask for prices, and pay for items in German.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to shopping in German! Asking about prices is simple: use **Wie viel kostet...?** for a single item (*Wie viel kostet das Brot?*) and **Wie viel kosten...?** for plurals (*Wie viel kosten die Äpfel?*).

When you reach the register (**die Kasse**), cashiers frequently ask: **"Bar oder mit Karte?"** (Cash or card?). Cash is still very popular in Germany, especially at local bakeries and open-air markets (**der Markt**).

*Helpful tip:* Most supermarkets charge for shopping bags (**die Tasche**), so locals almost always bring their own reusable bags! Also, note that most retail stores in Germany remain closed on Sundays.

exercises.translation: I would like to buy a bag.
We are going to the market today.

units.title: Weather
units.description: Talk about current weather conditions, temperatures, and the seasons of the year.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About the Weather
In German, weather expressions often start with the impersonal pronoun **es** (it):
- *Es ist kalt.* (It is cold.)
- *Es regnet.* (It is raining.)
- *Es schneit.* (It is snowing.)

### The Four Seasons
All four seasons in German are masculine and use the article **der**: *der Frühling* (spring), *der Sommer* (summer), *der Herbst* (autumn), and *der Winter* (winter). When saying 'in summer' or 'in winter', combine *in* + *dem* into **im**:
- *im Sommer* (in summer)
- *im Winter* (in winter)

### Quick Tip!
If you feel hot or cold, say **Mir ist kalt** or **Mir ist heiß** (literally: 'To me it is cold/hot'). Saying *Ich bin heiß* has a very different meaning!

units.title: Work & School
units.description: Talk about jobs, daily work routines, classes, and school life in German.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Jobs & School in German

When stating your profession in German, you typically **omit the article**! While English requires "I am *a* doctor", German speakers simply say **"Ich bin Arzt"** or **"Ich bin Ärztin"**.

#### Job Titles and Gender
Most job titles change based on gender by adding the suffix **-in** for women (and sometimes adding an umlaut):
- **der Lehrer** (male teacher) → **die Lehrerin** (female teacher)
- **der Student** (male student) → **die Studentin** (female student)

#### Everyday Locations
Pay attention to handy preposition contractions when talking about your daily routine:
- **zur Schule** (to school)
- **zur Arbeit** (to work)
- **im Büro** (in the office)

exercises.translation: I am going to school now.

exercises.answer: The doctor works in the hospital.

units.title: Health
units.description: Talk about your body, express aches, and describe how you feel.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Health in German

When you don't feel well, German offers simple ways to express it!

To describe pain, use the separable verb **wehtun** (to hurt):
- *Mein Kopf tut weh.* (My head hurts.)
- *Meine Augen tun weh.* (My eyes hurt – notice plural *tun*!)

To describe how you are feeling, combine **sein** (to be) with adjectives:
- *Ich bin müde.* (I am tired.)
- *Er ist krank.* (He is sick.)

When heading to get help, pay attention to contracted prepositions:
- **zum Arzt** (to the doctor – *zu* + *dem*)
- **ins Krankenhaus** (into the hospital – *in* + *das*)

Gute Besserung (Get well soon)!

exercises.answer: He is going to the doctor.

exercises.translation: We have to drive to the hospital.

exercises.answer: I am taking the medicine now.
